newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn seeks to stop war pensions to Nazi criminals.
newsitem.headline: Bonn seeks to stop war pensions to Nazi criminals.

text.p: Germany said on Wednesday it was doing all it could to stop disability pensions being paid to convicted Nazi war criminals after a U.S. Jewish group said thousands of these benefits were still being distributed.
"The German government and parliament are looking for ways to bar war criminals from receiving war-victim pensions," Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl said in a statement.

The government admitted in January that some Nazi war criminals were still receiving pensions after a television network said billions of marks (dollars) were being paid in disability pensions to them every year.

The American Jewish Committee said in an advert in Wednesday's New York Times that in the United States alone 3,377 pensions were sent each month to veterans of the armies of the Third Reich or their dependents.

"The German government provides generous monthly pensions to Nazi war veterans, whose injuries or even mild, chronic ailments qualify them for 'war victims pensions'," the committee said in its advert.

The explosive issue of pension payments to war criminals surfaced in December, when the World Jewish Congress called on Germany to publish the names of former members of Adolf Hitler's Waffen SS elite forces who live in Britain and the United States and receive disability pensions.
The German government refused, saying strict data protection laws prevented it from releasing such a list of names.
Bohl on Wednesday said there were still a few such cases in Germany but explained that this was due to a law passed after the war aimed at keeping pension and criminal issues separate.

Bohl stressed that some Waffen SS veterans were still entitled to disability pensions. "The Waffen SS was not just made up of voluntary members, but many were forcibly recruited Germans and foreigners," he said.

The American Jewish Committee also complained that while Holocaust survivors in other parts of the world were eligible to receive German pensions, up to 20,000 survivors in eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union had never received any kind of pension from Bonn.
Bohl said he thought this criticism was unjust. "Over 50 years after the end of the war, the German governemt still credits this task (of compensating victims) with an unchanged high value," he said.
He said Germany had paid about 100 billion marks in compensation since the war for victims of Nazi injustice and said the sum would continue to rise in the next few years.
But campaigners complain that those in the East received one-off payments to a maximum of 1,000 marks while those living in Germany get about 500 marks a month.

Bohl listed recent agreements with countries including Russia, Poland and Ukraine for compensating victims of the Nazi regime and said the country was still working on settlements with other governments.
